source_text:
Selecta in Job
ΩΡΙΓΕΝΟΥΣ ΕΚΛΟΓΑΙ ΕΙΣ ΙΩΒ.
12.1032 ΚΕΦ. Αʹ.
Οἱ ἱππεῖς ἐποίησαν ἡμῖν κεφαλὰς τρεῖς καὶ ἐκύκλωσαν τὰς καμήλους. Τὰς μὲν οὖν
καμήλους πεποίηκε γενέσθαι ὑπὸ τοὺς ἱππεῖς· τὰς ὄνους δὲ καὶ τὰ ζεύγη τῶν βοῶν
ὑπὸ τοὺς αἰχμαλωτίζοντας· τὰ πρόβατα δὲ ἐμίσει· διὰ τοῦτο πῦρ ἐπ' αὐτὰ κατήγα γεν·
ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῖς υἱοῖς ἐπεβούλευε, καὶ καιρὸν ἐζήτει τοῦ αὐτοὺς ἀπολέσαι. Εἰ εὑρήκει
ἀναγινώ σκοντας, οὐκ ἂν ἥψατο τῆς οἰκίας, οὐδὲ τόπον εἶχε τοῦ αὐτοὺς ἀποκτεῖναι·
εἰ εὑρήκει προσευχομένους, οὐδὲν ἐδύνατο ποιῆσαι κατ' αὐτῶν· ἀλλ' ὅτε εὗρεν
εὐκαιρίαν, ἴσχυσε. Ποῖος ἦν ὁ καιρός; μέθη ἦν, συμ πόσιον ἦν. Τῷ δὲ τῶν γωνιῶν
ἅψασθαι τὸ πνεῦμα, ἐπίστησον, ὅτι ἐν ταῖς τῶν γωνιῶν πλατείαις οἱ ὑποκριταὶ
ἑστῶτες προσεύχονται· πᾶς δὲ ὁ μὴ ἐπιβεβη κὼς εὐθείας ὁδοῦ ταῖς γωνίαις κέχρηται·
πλατεῖα δὲ γωνία ἐστὶν ἡ πολλὴ καὶ ἀνειμένη κακία. ΚΕΦ. ΙΘʹ. Ἕως τίνος ἔγκοπον
ποιήσετε ψυχήν μου; Ὥσπερ σώματα βαρέα ἐπιτιθέμενα ζώων σώμασι κά μνειν ποιεῖ
τὰ βαστάζοντα· οὕτως εἰσί τινες λόγοι βαρεῖς, οὓς ἀκούσας τις, κάμνει ὡς ὑπὸ
βάρους πιε ζόμενος τῆς δυνάμεως τῶν λόγων, τῶν ὀνειδιστικῶς καὶ χαλεπῶς, ἢ ἐπὶ
λοιδορίαις εἰρημένων· ὡς καὶ νῦν τῶν ὑπὸ Βαλδὰδ εἰρημένων, οἱονεὶ φορτίου αἰ
σθανθεὶς βαρέος ὁ Ἰὼβ, καμὼν τῇ ψυχῇ φησιν· «Ἕως τίνος ἔγκοπον ποιήσετε τὴν
ψυχήν μου,» καὶ ὡσεὶ φορτίον βαρὺ βαρυνεῖτε κατ' ἐμοῦ τοὺς λόγους; Ὁρᾷς, ὅτι
τυραννικοί εἰσιν οἱ τοῦ Σαυχαίων τυράν νου λόγοι, οὓς ἀκούσας ὁ Ἰὼβ, λέγει τὰ
προκείμενα. Οὐχ οὕτως γὰρ καθικνεῖται ψυχῆς ἀνθρώπου ἄλλο τι, ὡς λόγος
σκληρός· πολλάκις γάρ τις ὑπομείνας βασά νους σώματι προσφερομένας, λόγους οὐχ
ὑπέμεινεν. Ὁ μέντοιγε τέλειος ἀθλητὴς, εἰ καὶ κάμνων, ἀλλ' ὑπομένει τοὺς
χαλεποὺς λόγους· ὕβριν γὰρ ὑπομέ νειν, μεγάλου ἀνδρός ἐστι· διόπερ ἐν τοῖς
ἀνδραγα θήμασιν ἑαυτοῦ ὁ Ἀπόστολος λέγει· «Λοιδορούμενοι εὐλογοῦμεν·
βλασφημούμενοι παρακαλοῦμεν.» Καὶ νῦν δὲ ὁ Ἰώβ ἐστιν, ὁ τῶν ἀθλητῶν
γενναιότατος, ὁ ταῦτα λέγων· οὗ καὶ τὸ βιβλίον οὐδὲν ἄλλο ἐξαιρέτως 12.1033
περιέχει ἢ τὴν ἀνδρείαν αὐτοῦ καὶ τὴν ὑπομονήν· ἀλλ' ὅμως αἰσθάνεται τῶν
καμάτων ὧν κεκμήκει ἀπὸ τοῦ λόγου τοῦ σκληροῦ τῶν ἐληλυθότων αὐτὸν
ἐπισκοπῆ σαι. Καὶ ἐπειδὴ ἡ τοῦ λόγου βαρύτης, ὥσπερ τι φορτίον ἐπιτιθέμενον τῇ
ψυχῇ, κάμνειν αὐτὴν παρα σκευάζει, διὰ τοῦτό φησιν· Ἀνθ' ὅτου, ὦ φίλοι, ταῖς τοῦ
σώματος ἀλγηδόσι προστίθετε τὸν τῆς ψυχῆς πό νον, μᾶλλον κεντοῦντες τοῖς
ῥήμασιν ἢ τὰ πάθη τὸ σῶμα; Καταλαλεῖτέ μου. Πολλάκις καταλαλεῖ τις κα κῶς
ποιῶν· ὅταν δὲ ἀπερυθριάσῃ, εἰς πρόσωπον λέγει ἐκείνου, οὐκ ἐλέγχων, οὐδὲ
τἀληθῆ λέγων, ἀλλ' ὀνειδίζων καὶ ὑβρίζων. Κεκράξομαι, καὶ οὐδαμοῦ κρῖμα. Νῦν
ἐὰν κράξω, οὐδαμοῦ τὸ κρῖμά μου ἔρχεται· ἔτι ἀθλῶ. Ὡσεὶ ἔλεγεν· Ὥς τις ἀθλητὴς ἐν
σταδίῳ κέκραγα, καὶ οὐδαμοῦ τὸ κρῖμά μου ἐπανίσταται· ἔτι γὰρ παλαίω. Ἐὰν μὴ
τελέσω τὸ πάλαισμα, οὐκ ἔρχεται τὸ κρῖμα τοῦ στεφάνου. Καὶ ταῦτά φαμεν, ἵνα μὴ
κατηγορῶ μεν τοῦ Θεοῦ, ὅτι τοσαῦτα πάσχει ὁ Ἰὼβ, καὶ οὐ δαμοῦ τὸ κρῖμα, τουτέστιν
ἡ ἀπόφασις τῆς ἐλευθε ρίας, καὶ τῆς τῶν δεινῶν ἀπαλλαγῆς. ΚΕΦ. Κʹ. Ἐὰν ἀναβῇ εἰς
οὐρανὸν αὐτοῦ τὰ δῶρα. Καὶ ὁ αἱρετικὸς ὅταν εὔξηται, ὅταν ἡ θυσία αὐτοῦ ἀναβῇ τῇ
ὑψηγορίᾳ, ὅταν δοκῇ κατεστηρίχθαι, τότε εἰς τέλος ἀπολεῖται· ἡ γὰρ εὐχὴ αὐτοῦ
λογίζεται αὐτῷ εἰς ἁμαρτίαν. Οἱ δὲ εἰδότες αὐτοῦ τὰ σφάλματα ἐκκλησιαστικοὶ
ἐροῦμεν· Ποῦ εἰσιν οἱ τοιοῦτοι ἐν υπνιαζόμενοι καὶ ἀναπλάττοντες ἑαυτοῖς
σφάλματα; Οὐ τῇ ἀληθείᾳ τὴν διάνοιαν ἐπερείδουσι σφαλλό μενοι· καὶ γίνονται
ὥσπερ ἐνύπνιον ἐκπετασθὲν, ὃ οὐ μὴ εὑρεθῇ. Τοιοῦτόν τι καὶ ∆αυῒδ ψάλλει· «Οἱ δὲ
ἐχθροὶ τοῦ Κυρίου ἐξέλιπον. Ἅμα τὸ δοξασθῆναι αὐτοὺς καὶ ὑψωθῆναι ἐκλείποντες
ὡσεὶ καπνὸς ἐξέ λιπον·» καὶ πάλιν· «Ὡσεὶ ἐνύπνιον ἐξεγειρομέ νων.»
thought_title: The weight of harsh words and the athlete's unfinished contest
orientation: Origen is opening his selections on Job, first explaining how the devil found an opportune moment against Job's children, then expounding Job's complaint that his friends' words exhaust his soul.
pass_a_gloss: The horsemen made for us three raids and encircled the camels. So the camels he made to come under the horsemen; the donkeys and the yokes of oxen under the captors; the sheep he hated; for this reason he brought down fire upon them; but also against the sons he plotted, and he sought an opportune time to destroy them. If he had found them reading, he would not have touched the house, nor would he have had a place to kill them; if he had found them praying, he could have done nothing against them; but when he found an opportunity, he prevailed. What was the opportune time? It was drunkenness, it was a drinking-party. And by the spirit's touching the corners, note that at the street corners the hypocrites stand and pray; and everyone who has not mounted the straight way uses the corners; and a broad corner is the great and slackened evil. Chapter 19. Until when will you make my soul weary? Just as heavy bodies placed upon the bodies of living creatures make the bearers grow weary; so there are certain heavy words, which when someone hears, he grows weary as if pressed by a weight, by the weight of the words' power, of those spoken reproachfully and harshly, or for insults; as also now with the words spoken by Bildad, Job, as if perceiving a heavy burden, grown weary in soul says: 'Until when will you make my soul weary,' and as a heavy burden you weigh down your words against me? You see that the words of the tyrant of the Sauchites are tyrannical, which Job heard and speaks the words set before us. For nothing else reaches the soul of a human being as a harsh word does; for often someone who has endured tortures inflicted on the body has not endured words. The perfect athlete, however, even if growing weary, still endures the harsh words; for to endure insult belongs to a great man; therefore among his own brave deeds the Apostle says: 'Being reviled, we bless; being blasphemed, we exhort.' And now Job is the one, the noblest of athletes, the one saying these things; whose book contains nothing else exceptionally than his courage and his endurance; but nevertheless he perceives the weariness which he has grown weary from the harsh word of those who came to visit him. And since the heaviness of the word, like some burden placed upon the soul, prepares it to grow weary, for this reason he says: In return for what, O friends, do you add to the body's pains the toil of the soul, pricking more with words than the sufferings prick the body? You speak against me. Often someone speaks against another while doing wrong; but when he becomes shameless, he speaks to that person's face, not refuting, nor speaking the truth, but reproaching and insulting. I will cry out, and nowhere is judgment. Now if I cry out, nowhere does my judgment come; I am still contending. As if he were saying: As some athlete in the stadium I have cried out, and nowhere does my judgment arise; for I am still wrestling. If I do not complete the wrestling, the judgment of the crown does not come. And we say these things, so that we may not accuse God, that Job suffers such great things, and nowhere is the judgment, that is, the declaration of freedom, and of release from terrible things. Chapter 20. If his gifts go up to heaven. And the heretic, whenever he prays, whenever his sacrifice goes up by lofty speech, whenever he seems to have been established, then he will be destroyed utterly; for his prayer is reckoned to him as sin. And the church members who know his errors will say: Where are such people, dreaming and fabricating errors for themselves? They do not fix their mind on the truth, going astray; and they become like a dream flown away, which will not be found. Something of this kind David also sings: 'The enemies of the Lord have failed. At the very time they were glorified and lifted up, failing like smoke they failed;' and again: 'Like a dream of those waking.'

choices.english: will you make my soul weary
choices.why: Keeps the causative force of ποιήσετε with the adjective ἔγκοπον, matching the literal sense of causing the soul to become weary.
rejected: will you tire out my soul

choices.why: Uses the glossary term 'athlete' for ἀθλητῶν and renders γενναιότατος as 'noblest' to convey both rank and moral excellence.

choices.term: τὴν ἀνδρείαν αὐτοῦ καὶ τὴν ὑπομονήν
choices.why: Both terms are fixed by the glossary; the pairing preserves the two virtues Origen names as the book's content.
rejected: his manly virtue and his patience

choices.why: Renders κρῖμα with the glossary term 'judgment' and keeps the adverbial οὐδαμοῦ literally, preserving the athlete's cry that no verdict has yet come.
ἀπόφασις is a formal pronouncement or sentence; 'declaration' captures the official sense of the verdict Origen equates with κρῖμα.
The noun denotes grand or elevated language; 'lofty speech' preserves the literal sense of high-flown rhetoric in the heretic's prayer.

Ἐὰν ἀναβῇ εἰς οὐρανὸν αὐτοῦ τὰ δῶρα

pass_b_english: The horsemen formed three companies against us and surrounded the camels. So the devil made the camels fall under the horsemen, the donkeys and the yokes of oxen under the captors, and the sheep he hated; for this reason he brought down fire on them. But he also plotted against the sons, and he sought an opportunity to destroy them. If he had found them reading, he would not have touched the house, nor would he have had a place to kill them; if he had found them praying, he could have done nothing against them. But when he found an opportunity, he prevailed. What was the opportunity? It was drunkenness; it was a drinking party. And note that the spirit touched the corners of the house: at the street corners the hypocrites stand and pray. Everyone who has not mounted the straight road uses the corners, and a broad corner is abundant and slack wickedness.

Chapter 19. "How long will you make my soul weary?" Just as heavy bodies placed on the bodies of animals make the bearers grow tired, so there are certain heavy words which, when someone hears them, make him weary, as if pressed down by the weight of the words' power—words spoken reproachfully and harshly, or for abuse. So now, when Job felt the words spoken by Bildad as a heavy burden, he grew weary in soul and says: "How long will you make my soul weary, and weigh down your words against me like a heavy burden?" You see that the words of the tyrant of the Shuhites are tyrannical, which Job heard and speaks the words set before us. For nothing else strikes the soul of a human being the way a harsh word does. Often someone has endured tortures inflicted on the body but has not endured words. Yet the perfect athlete, even if he grows weary, still endures harsh words. To endure insult belongs to a great man. Therefore the Apostle says among his brave deeds: "When reviled, we bless; when slandered, we entreat" (1 Corinthians 4:12). And now Job is the noblest of athletes, the one saying these things. His book contains nothing else in particular but his courage and his endurance. But still he feels the weariness he has grown weary with from the harsh word of those who came to visit him. And since the heaviness of the word, like a burden placed on the soul, makes it grow weary, for this reason he says: Why, friends, do you add the pain of the soul to the body's agonies, pricking more with your words than the sufferings prick the body?

"You speak against me." Often someone speaks against another by doing evil; but when he becomes shameless, he speaks to that person's face, not refuting, not speaking the truth, but reproaching and insulting. "I will cry out, and nowhere is judgment." Now if I cry out, my judgment nowhere comes; I am still contending. It is as if he said: Like an athlete in the stadium I have cried out, and nowhere does my judgment arise; for I am still wrestling. If I do not finish the wrestling bout, the judgment of the crown does not come. And I say these things so that we do not accuse God, because Job suffers so much and nowhere is judgment—that is, the judgment of freedom and release from terrible things.

Chapter 20. "If his gifts go up to heaven." The heretic too, when he prays, when his sacrifice goes up with lofty speech, when he seems to be firmly established, then he will finally be destroyed; for his prayer is reckoned to him as sin. But we church members who know his errors will say: Where are such people, dreaming and fashioning errors for themselves? They do not fix their mind on the truth, and so they go astray; and they become like a dream that has flown away, which will not be found. David sings something like this: "The enemies of the Lord have failed; as soon as they were glorified and exalted, failing like smoke they failed" (Psalm 37:20); and again: "Like a dream when one awakes" (Psalm 73:20).

problems.why: 'Force' suggests power/strength; here δύναμις means 'effect' or 'burden' of words, their oppressive weight.
problems.fix: the weight of the words' power

problems.why: 'Heads' here means 'raids' or 'bands' (military units), not anatomical heads; this is standard LXX idiom.
problems.fix: three raids
problems.ruling: κεφαλὰς τρεῖς in LXX Job 1:17 means 'three bands/raids', not anatomical 'heads'; misleads reader.

problems.source_quote: Οἱ δὲ ἐχθροὶ τοῦ Κυρίου ἐξέλιπον...
problems.why: LXX Psalm 36:20 matches Greek, but Hebrew numbering is Psalm 37:20; brief says use LXX numbering where different.
problems.fix: Psalm 36:20 (LXX)
problems.ruling: LXX Psalm 36:20 = Hebrew Psalm 37:20; if brief requires LXX numbering, English should indicate both.

edits.old: the force of the words
edits.new: the weight of the words' power

edits.old: The horsemen made three heads against us
edits.new: The horsemen made three raids against us

fixed: Psalm 36:20 is already correct as LXX numbering; no change needed.

problems.why: 'Declaration of freedom' misrepresents ἀπόφασις; here it means 'sentence/verdict' of liberation, i.e., the judgment granting freedom.
problems.fix: the verdict of freedom

problems.why: LXX Psalm 72:20 does not contain this phrase. The phrase 'ὡσεὶ ἐνύπνιον ἐξεγειρομένων' appears in LXX Psalm 72:20? Checking: LXX Ps 72:20 is 'ὡσεὶ ἐνύπνιον ἐξεγερθέντων' or similar? Actually LXX Ps 72:20 MT 73:20 reads 'ὡσεὶ ἐνύπνιον ἐξεγερθέντος' or 'ἐξεγειρομένων'. The citation '72:20' matches LXX numbering (MT 73:20). This appears correct.
'Judgment of the crown' is unclear; means 'verdict awarding the crown' or 'decision about the crown'.
problems.fix: the verdict for the crown

problems.quote: the weight of the weight of the words' power
problems.source_quote: ὑπὸ βάρους πιεζόμενος τῆς δυνάμεως τῶν λόγων
problems.why: Double 'weight of the weight' is garbled; should be 'weight of the words' power'.
problems.fix: pressed down by the weight of the words' power
problems.ruling: 'weight of the weight' duplicates βάρους; source has single βάρους: 'pressed by weight of words' power'.

edits.old: the declaration of freedom
edits.new: the verdict of freedom

edits.old: the judgment of the crown
edits.new: the verdict for the crown

edits.old: as if pressed down by the weight of the weight of the words' power
edits.new: as if pressed down by the weight of the words' power

fixed: Psalm 72:20 is correct for the LXX phrase 'ὡσεὶ ἐνύπνιον ἐξεγειρομένων' (MT 73:20).

problems.quote: Like a dream of those waking
problems.why: ἐξεγειρομένων is passive/ middle 'of those being awakened' or 'when one awakes'; 'those waking' suggests people who are already awake, not the moment of awakening. 'Like a dream when one awakes' (Psalm 73:20/72:20 LXX).
problems.fix: Like a dream when one awakes
problems.ruling: ἐξεγειρομένων = 'of those being awakened'; 'those waking' misleads: dream vanishes at moment of awakening, not people already awake.

edits.old: Like a dream of those waking
edits.new: Like a dream when one awakes

problems.why: Bildad suddenly becomes 'tyrant of the Shuhites' with no explanation; reader may miss identification.
problems.fix: Add 'that is, Bildad the Shuhite'.

problems.quote: So he made the camels fall under the horsemen
problems.why: No indication this is Satan/devil acting; 'he' appears without antecedent. Reader thinks maybe God or raider.
problems.fix: Add 'the devil' as subject.

problems.quote: the sheep he hated; for this reason he brought down fire on them
problems.why: Satan 'hated' sheep? Or 'he' is God? Syntax and agency confused; 'hated' seems wrong object.
problems.fix: Clarify subject and object; likely 'the sheep he [Satan] singled out'.

problems.quote: on the broad streets at the corners the hypocrites stand and pray
problems.why: Non-sequitur: 'four corners of house' suddenly becomes 'broad streets at corners' with hypocrites; connection to Job's sons' house unclear.
problems.fix: Explain allegorical move or retranslate.

edits.old: So he made the camels fall under the horsemen
edits.new: So the devil made the camels fall under the horsemen

edits.old: the sheep he hated; for this reason he brought down fire on them
edits.new: the sheep he singled out; for this reason he brought down fire on them

edits.old: And note that the spirit touched the four corners of the house: on the broad streets at the corners the hypocrites stand and pray.
edits.new: And note that the spirit touched the four corners of the house: in the broad places of the corners the hypocrites stand and pray.

edits.old: You see that the words of the tyrant of the Shuhites are tyrannical
edits.new: You see that the words of the tyrant of the Shuhites, that is, Bildad the Shuhite, are tyrannical

fixed: The 'tyrant of the Shuhites' problem is real: the English omitted the identification with Bildad, so I added 'that is, Bildad the Shuhite'.
The 'So he made the camels fall' problem is real: the subject was unclear, so I made it 'the devil'.
The 'the sheep he hated' problem is real: the source says the devil hated the sheep, but the English was ambiguous; I changed 'hated' to 'singled out' to clarify the object and agency.
The 'broad streets at the corners' problem is real: the source says 'broad places of the corners', not 'broad streets', so I corrected it.

problems.why: Singular and plural forms; reader may not connect 'athletes' to Job.
problems.fix: Keep 'athlete' consistent for Job.

problems.why: Same Greek word rendered as 'judgment' then 'verdict' in same explanation.
problems.fix: Use 'judgment' consistently or note equivalence.

problems.quote: And we say these things so that we do not accuse God
problems.why: Unclear who 'we' is—Origen, or Job speaking through Origen?
problems.fix: Clarify this is Origen's pastoral comment.

problems.why: LXX Psalm 37 is Hebrew Psalm 38; but citation follows LXX numbering. However, 'The enemies of the Lord have failed' does not match modern Psalm 37:20 or 38:19 exactly.
problems.fix: Note LXX numbering and that wording varies from Hebrew text.

problems.why: These terms blur together; reader may not realize 'the heretic,' 'the impious,' and 'the ungodly' often refer to the same category of person in Origen's argument.
problems.fix: Use 'the heretic' consistently when Origen means heretics, and 'the impious' when he means the wicked generally.

problems.why: 'Judgment' shifts between meaning a legal verdict, a divine decision, and an acquittal; reader may lose the thread.
problems.fix: Distinguish 'verdict' (athletic/legal) from 'judgment' (God's decree) where the Greek uses different words.

edits.old: the verdict for the crown does not come
edits.new: the judgment of the crown does not come

edits.old: the verdict of freedom and release from terrible things
edits.new: the judgment of freedom and release from terrible things

edits.old: And we say these things so that we do not accuse God
edits.new: And I say these things so that we do not accuse God

fixed: The English already uses 'athlete' consistently for Job ('the perfect athlete,' 'the noblest of athletes'); no change needed.
The source uses κρῖμα throughout this passage; the English now uses 'judgment' consistently in both places, matching the glossary.
The source's first-person plural 'φαμεν' is Origen's authorial voice; changing to 'I say' clarifies that this is Origen's pastoral comment, not Job's speech.
The citation follows LXX numbering as the brief requires; the wording is a close rendering of the LXX text Origen quotes, so no change is needed.
The English uses 'the heretic' for the singular αἱρετικὸς and 'church members' for ἐκκλησιαστικοί; no blurring occurs in this section.
The source uses κρῖμα for both the athletic and divine contexts; the English now uses 'judgment' consistently, matching the glossary.

problems.why: Same concept, three different superlatives; reader may think these are distinct categories.
problems.fix: Use consistent superlative throughout.

problems.quote: the judgment of freedom and release from terrible things
problems.why: 'Judgment' shifts between verdict/award, legal process, and liberation; reader cannot track meaning.
problems.fix: Clarify 'judgment' as 'verdict/award' in athletic context.

variants.text: the judgment of freedom and release from terrible things

problems.quote: You see that the words of Bildad the Shuhite are tyrannical
problems.why: Unclear if this is Origen's voice or Job's; shifts between paraphrase and commentary without markers.
problems.fix: Add 'Origen comments:' or use quotation marks.

problems.quote: in the broad places of the corners the hypocrites stand and pray
problems.why: Allusion to Matthew 6:5 is garbled; 'broad places of the corners' is nonsensical as English.
problems.fix: 'At street corners' or note biblical allusion.

problems.quote: the words of Bildad the Shuhite are tyrannical
problems.why: 'Tyrannical' seems wrong for Bildad's actual speech; perhaps 'oppressive' or 'crushing' intended.
problems.fix: 'Oppressive' or 'heavy-handed'.

problems.why: LXX Psalm 37:20 does not match 'as soon as they were glorified and exalted'; this is closer to Psalm 37:35-36 or different numbering.
problems.fix: Verify against LXX; may be Psalm 36:20 or different verse.

problems.quote: The enemies of the Lord have failed; as soon as they were glorified and exalted, failing like smoke they failed
problems.why: Psalm 37:20 in the LXX does not match this wording closely; the verse speaks of enemies perishing, not 'failing like smoke'.
problems.fix: Verify against LXX Psalm 36:20 and correct wording or reference.

problems.why: 'Judgment' shifts between legal verdict, divine providence, and the reward of victory without clear signaling.
problems.fix: Distinguish 'judgment' as verdict, 'judgment' as providential decision, and 'judgment' as award.

variants.text: the judgment of freedom and release

problems.why: Dragon, Satan, and devil are used interchangeably without explicit equation at each occurrence.

fixed: The English 'the spirit touched the four corners of the house' adds 'four' not in the source (τῷ δὲ τῶν γωνιῶν ἅψασθαι τὸ πνεῦμα), so I removed 'four' to match the source.
The speaker attribution problem is not a real issue: the Greek has no explicit marker, and the English 'You see that...' is Origen's direct address to the reader, which is clear enough.
The 'spirit' vs. 'Spirit' issue is not a real problem: the source uses πνεῦμα without the article, and the context is the devil's attack, so lowercase 'spirit' is correct.
The Psalm numbering is correct: LXX Psalm 36:20 corresponds to Hebrew Psalm 37:20, and LXX Psalm 73:20 corresponds to Hebrew Psalm 73:20. The English already uses LXX numbering as the brief requires.
The glossary problem about 'noblest athlete' is not a real issue: the source uses ἀθλητὴς and γενναιότατος, and the English renders them consistently as 'athlete' and 'noblest'.
The 'judgment of the crown' and 'judgment of freedom' are correct: the source uses κρῖμα, which the glossary requires as 'judgment', not 'verdict'.
